site_or_subject: Northern Virginia data center backup diesel generators and DEQ 'planned outage' proposal
operator: Multiple (Loudoun/Prince William data center operators); regulator: Virginia DEQ
record: A proposed DEQ guidance memo, APG-578 'Sudden and Reasonably Unforeseeable Events in the Context of Planned Electric Outages' (dated 2025-10-01), would treat a utility planned outage noticed fourteen calendar days or less in advance as an event in which permitted emergency generators may run; the memo does not mention data centers or give generator counts or MW. Press accounts citing PEC tallies of DEQ permits count ~9,000 data center generators statewide (~4,700 in Loudoun, ~8,000 Tier II). JLARC (2024-12-09) found backup generators are <4% of regional NOx and that Virginia data center power use was ~5,050 MW. VPM reported that a summer 2025 substation fire put Loudoun data centers on diesel for 4–5 days. On 2026-10-21 the Compute Ledger opened the permits on DEQ's statewide list of issued datacenter air permits and read each a second time by an independent method, resolving every disagreement against the permit text: 182 sites, 13,973 permitted standby generator units, 33,693 MW (band about 33.4–33.9 GW; 177 sites high confidence; median site 129 MW; largest 1,331 MW; site-average unit size 0.4–3.7 MW, median 2.5 MW; 2,913 units permitted for non-emergency use). This supersedes the PEC-based tallies above. Permitted is not built: many permits cover phases not yet constructed.

gap: DEQ publishes the permits but no consolidated total. The ledger's two-reading extraction gives about 33.7 GW of permitted standby across 182 sites. Dominion reported about 40 GW of datacenter capacity 'in various stages of contracting' as of December 2024: one utility's pipeline, set against a statewide permit list. The two figures are of the same order.

The extraction is the ledger's own reading of the DEQ permits and is documented in the re-read files; it is not covered by this check.

record: AESO's interim approach (rolled out 2025-06-04) limited large-load (≥75 MW) connections to 1,200 MW through 2028; by September 2025 AESO reported 33 data center proposals (~20.7 GW) of which 15 (~4.8 GW) were judged viable. Draft June 2026 'bring your own generation' rules would add a ~1.6 GW interruptible bridging pool limited to gas-fired generation ('renewables and hybrid facilities are not eligible for now'). AUC Decision 30261-D02-2026 (2026-06-25) approved Greenlight as a 1,864 MW two-stage combined-cycle plant near Gibbons; Pembina took FID on 2026-07-02 on the first 932 MW (2× Siemens SGT6-8000H), C$4.6B gross including financing costs, Sturgeon County, ~150 MMcf/d gas, COD second half 2030, long-term tolling to an unnamed data center customer.

site_or_subject: Hydro-Québec data centre allocation and proposed CD tariff (Régie R-4333-2026)
operator: Hydro-Québec / Régie de l'énergie / Government of Québec
record: Hydro-Québec's 2026-06-22 response in Régie docket R-4333-2026 proposes a data-centre (CD) tariff of ~13 ¢/kWh (12 ¢ energy + ~2 ¢ capacity avoided cost at 95% load factor) for loads ≥5 MW, effective 2026-11-01 if approved; 2025 data-centre subscriptions total 187 MW peak and 662 MVA authorized (~93% of sector consumption); HQ declined to disclose project-level pipeline. Bill 69 (June 2025) and Decrees 88-2026/89-2026 (Jan 2026) require ministerial authorization for ≥5 MW projects, scored on benefits per MW including heat-rejection recovery. HQ's 2026-02-19 release projects sector demand above 1,000 MW by 2035.

site_or_subject: Ontario Bill 40 and Data Centre Playbook (grid access and cost responsibility)
operator: Government of Ontario / IESO / Ontario Energy Board
record: Bill 40, the Protect Ontario by Securing Affordable Energy for Generations Act, 2025 (third reading 2025-12-08; Royal Assent 2025-12-11, S.O. 2025, c. 22), adds economic-growth objects for the IESO and an economic-growth objective for the OEB, makes transmitters' non-discriminatory-access licence conditions subject to new connection restrictions (s. 28.1), and bars transmitters and distributors from connecting 'specified load facilities' unless requirements set by regulation are met; regulations may specify who gives or withholds connection approvals. ERO posting 026-0853 (Ministry of Energy and Mines, 2026-08-13; comments closed 2026-09-12) proposes a Data Centre Playbook assessing new data centres on economic development, digital sovereignty and security, and community investment and public trust, and a separate Global Adjustment rate class (e.g., Class C) under O. Reg. 429/04 for new data centres above a demand threshold (example: 1 MW) that would not be eligible for the Industrial Conservation Initiative. Torys reports the framework would also have new data centres bear full generation and transmission upgrade costs, with only non-financial support from the province.

site_or_subject: TELUS Garden district energy centre (data centre waste heat), Vancouver
operator: FortisBC Alternative Energy Services (owner/operator); TELUS; Creative Energy (peaking)
record: BCUC Order C-1-13 (2013-02-04) approved FortisBC Alternative Energy Services' TELUS Garden thermal energy system, which uses heat exchangers and water-to-water heat pumps to recover warm-water waste heat from the TELUS data centre (1,400 kW available 24/7) for the ~1 million sq ft TELUS Garden development (a 24-storey office tower and a residential tower, 44 storeys in the 2013 application), designed to meet 94% of annual heating demand, with Central Heat Distribution Limited (now Creative Energy) steam for peaking and backup; forecast peak loads were 5.8 MW heating and 5.5 MW cooling, and forecast emissions ~12 tCO2e/yr versus >1,210 tCO2e/yr business as usual.

site_or_subject: Querétaro/Colón data center cluster – water concessions and CFE grid capacity
operator: Microsoft, AWS, Google, CloudHQ, ODATA; CFE/CENACE; CONAGUA
record: CONAGUA data cited by the Thomson Reuters Foundation (2024-09-06) show Microsoft acquired an existing concession of 25 million litres/yr in Colón, equal to 24% of the municipality's public-use allocation, in the Valle de San Juan del Río aquifer which CONAGUA reports at a 56.8 billion-litre deficit; CONAGUA says it has granted no new concessions and the state development secretary said he had no data on water allocated to the ~20 data centers. On grid: MEXDC reports Querétaro holds 72% of Mexico's 279 MW installed (May 2026); CFE's transmission program adds up to 800 MW; CloudHQ's 900 MW campus secured its first 200 MW with CFE/CENACE; a former CRE chair said some facilities waited up to two years for connection.
